findings.where: Why the Word Is So Tempting, paragraph 3, sentence 1: "The sociologists Bradley Campbell and Jason Manning have written about what happens when that instinct comes loose from its source."
findings.problem: (a)/(f) This attributes a view to two living scholars that no ledger line supports. The sentence says they wrote about the Christian-taught regard for victims (Holland's thesis, the paragraph before) coming loose from Christianity. Ledger line 119 verifies only their thesis about victimhood culture. Two searches this run found nothing tracing their account to Christianity, and the publisher's description says the conflicts they describe are not religious-versus-secular. The link between Holland and Campbell-Manning is the essay's own reading, but the sentence presents it as theirs.
findings.fix: Replace the sentence with: "The sociologists Bradley Campbell and Jason Manning describe what looks like that instinct come loose from its source."

findings.where: Why the Word Is So Tempting, paragraph 3, sentence 2: "Their book *The Rise of Victimhood Culture* argues that a newer moral culture grants the highest moral standing to victims, which gives people a reason to publicize the offenses against them."
findings.problem: (c) The word "highest" is not shown by any source. Ledger line 119 cites Wikipedia, Palgrave and catalogs for the incentive to publicize grievances, but none of its quoted wording says "highest". Two searches this run summarize the authors as saying that publicizing an offense lowers the offender's moral status and "raises the moral status of the victims". That is a gain in status, not the top rank.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Their book *The Rise of Victimhood Culture* argues that in a newer moral culture being a victim raises a person's moral standing, which gives people a reason to publicize the offenses against them."

findings.where: Who Has Been Persecuted in America, Saul paragraph, last sentence: "The persecutors in Scripture are rarely cynics, and most of them are sure they are right."
findings.problem: (a) This claim has no ledger line, and the text cuts against it. In the site's BSB text, Herod seizes Peter because killing James pleased the people (Acts 12:3). The slave-girl's owners act when their profit is gone (Acts 16:19). Demetrius defends his trade (Acts 19:24-27). The chief priests hand Jesus over out of envy (Mark 15:10). Pilate acts to satisfy the crowd (Mark 15:15). Jealousy drives Acts 5:17, 13:45 and 17:5. A reader who knows Acts will catch the overclaim.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Some of the fiercest persecutors in Scripture were sure they were right."

findings.where: What the New Testament Means by the Word, paragraph 3: ""Rejoice and be glad," Jesus said (Matthew 5:12), and a few verses later, "Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you" (5:44)."
findings.problem: (c)/(e) Matthew 5:44 comes 32 verses after 5:12, so "a few verses later" is wrong. The ledger (line 75) checks the wording of both quotations, which is exact ESV, but not this position claim.
findings.fix: Change "and a few verses later," to "and later in the same sermon,".

findings.where: Who Has Been Persecuted in America, Saul paragraph, sentence 2: "The most famous persecutor in the Bible was a devout man defending God."
findings.problem: (a) This is a small overstatement with no ledger line. Pharaoh or Herod could fairly claim the title "most famous persecutor in the Bible". The claim is true of the persecutors of the church.
findings.fix: Replace with: "The New Testament's most famous persecutor was a devout man defending God."

findings.where: The Cases Christians Point To, paragraph 2: "The memo leaked a few weeks later."
findings.problem: (c) Ledger lines 60-61 date the memo January 23, 2023 and the leak February 8, 2023. That is sixteen days, which is closer to two weeks than to a few weeks.
findings.fix: Replace with: "The memo leaked about two weeks later."

findings.where: The Cases Christians Point To, paragraph 1: "The mayor said the problem was judgment and insubordination: Cochran had not gotten the required permission to publish, and the book had compromised his ability to lead gay employees."
findings.problem: (f) The sentence correctly attributes the reasons to the mayor. But the permission point is contested, and the essay gives only the city's side about a living man. Ledger line 57 records that Cochran says he had permission from the ethics office. A search this run (WABE, ADF and others) reports that Cochran said the director of Atlanta's Ethics Office gave him permission, while the city's investigation found he did not seek approval.
findings.fix: Replace with: "The mayor said the problem was judgment and insubordination: Cochran had not gotten the required permission to publish (Cochran said the head of the city's ethics office had given it), and the book had compromised his ability to lead gay employees."

findings.where: The Cases Christians Point To, paragraph 1: "a devotional book for men that taught the traditional Christian view of sex and marriage"
findings.problem: (f) This is still open as a Note for James in ledger line 56. The essay describes the book the way its defenders do. A search this run (Baptist Press, Christian Post, Rough Draft Atlanta) reports a passage, on page 82 according to Rough Draft, that defined uncleanness as including homosexuality, lesbianism, pederasty and bestiality. Outlets differ on the exact punctuation. The essay's wording is accurate, but it is the milder half of the story, and the skeptic reader may notice that the city's side is softened.
findings.fix: James's call; no change is required. If he wants the city's side stated more fully, add after the sentence, as paraphrase with no quotation marks: "Critics pointed to a passage that listed homosexuality, along with pederasty and bestiality, among forms of sexual uncleanness."

findings.where: Opening, paragraph 4: "In 2024 the Pew Research Center found that 48 percent of American adults felt at least some conflict between their religious beliefs and mainstream culture, up from 42 percent in 2020."
findings.problem: The sentence is accurate as written (ledger line 48; reconfirmed this run). A newer figure exists: Pew's report of October 20, 2025 (survey February 3-9, 2025) puts the share at 58 percent, 10 points above 2024 and 16 above 2020. The ledger's Note for James already flags this. No integrity fault.
findings.fix: Optional, James's call. Append: ", and by early 2025 the share had reached 58 percent" before the final period.

findings.problem: (c), ledger only. The line quotes the interpretive sentence as "A culture formed that way listens ...", but the essay now reads "A culture formed that way takes it seriously when someone says he has been wronged." The ledger is stale; the essay makes no new factual claim here.
findings.fix: No essay change. Update ledger line 118 to quote the current sentence.
